analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices, backed by 34 senators, never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law forbids Medicare from using its buying power to negotiate drug prices directly. This bill would delete that ban and let the government negotiate prices for drugs covered by Medicare's prescription drug benefit. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million seniors and disabled people on Medicare who pay for prescription drugs, either out of pocket or through premiums and cost-sharing. If the government negotiates lower prices, those savings flow to beneficiaries and to the federal budget, which funds the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the current legal ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices directly with manufacturers for drugs covered under the Part D benefit [S2] [S3].
Lets the government also set the price structure for reimbursing those drugs, so negotiated prices actually flow through the program [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who currently sell into Medicare at prices they set themselves, would face a single large buyer negotiating prices down. Some reduction in industry profits and possibly in research spending would follow.

drawbacks.text: The bill is short — it simply strikes the non-negotiation clause [S3] — and leaves open how prices would be set, which critics of negotiation generally worry could mean prices set more by government formula than by market bargaining.

Lower negotiated prices mean less revenue for pharmaceutical manufacturers, which the industry argues would reduce investment in new drug development; that tradeoff is the core honest objection to any Medicare negotiation bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain for seniors is straightforward: Medicare is the largest purchaser of prescription drugs in the country, and every other large buyer negotiates. The cost is reduced drug-company revenue and some risk of slower innovation on new drugs. On balance, giving Medicare the same negotiating power any private insurer already has is a net win for the tens of millions of people the program covers, though the bill's one-line approach left the hard details of how prices get set unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and it stayed there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote through the end of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Klobuchar introduced the bill on March 18, 2021, with 34 original cosponsors, all Democrats or the independent Sen. King [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that is the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2023, without the Finance Committee taking the bill up or the Senate voting on it [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the current law that bars Medicare from negotiating, so they continued selling at prices they set. Medicare beneficiaries kept paying more than they would have under negotiated prices.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let the HHS Secretary negotiate Medicare drug prices.

for.name: 33 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a majority of the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but as committee chair never scheduled a markup or brought it to a committee vote; the bill died at referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices throughout this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent King; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split was recorded [S4].

industries.note: The bill strikes the clause that forbids Medicare from negotiating drug prices, letting the government's buying power push prices below what manufacturers currently charge [S2] [S3]. That is why drug makers lobbied hard against Medicare negotiation during this era; their gain from the status quo is seniors' higher cost.

industries.industry: Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill lets HHS set the reimbursement price structure for drugs covered under Part D, which would push the middlemen who currently run drug pricing down the chain and could shrink their negotiating role [S2].
